comparison: Both strongly support the methodology (C17-C115). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive documentation, substantial sample size, and reproducibility. Peer reviewers praised the 'comprehensive approach' and 'impressive data collection.' Peer review also includes statistical methodology claims (C116-C123) that OpenEval evaluates separately in R21.

OpenEval R21 evaluates statistical methodology (C116-C123) as supported with appropriate methods. Peer review R1 includes these claims in their overall methodological approval without separate discussion.

Perfect agreement on C21-C23. Both confirm statistically significant differences in landing force between hunting strikes and perching events. OpenEval highlights the large sample size and highly significant p-value; peer reviewer explicitly confirmed the finding without concerns.

Strong agreement on environmental effects on landing force (C24-C31, C55). Both support the temporal pattern and substrate differences. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor (GAMM, p-values, confidence intervals); peer reviewer explicitly acknowledged all findings including force reduction approaching hunting attempts. Peer review also includes C32 and C88 which OpenEval addresses separately.

OpenEval R4 addresses temporal pattern in perch selection (C32) as supported but requiring interpretation. Peer review R3 includes C32 among accepted environmental findings without distinguishing it as more interpretive.

Both support the relationship between landing force and hunting success for sit-and-wait strategy (C51-C52, C54, C61). OpenEval notes modest effect size and low R-squared, acknowledging limitations. Peer reviewer concluded 'results support the authors' conclusion' and editor found evidence 'compelling.' Peer review also includes C50 and C53 which OpenEval addresses separately.

OpenEval R6 evaluates C50 (no relationship for hunting on the wing) as important negative result establishing specificity. Peer review R4 includes C50 in overall acceptance of hunting success findings without separate discussion of this negative result.

Perfect agreement on C33-C35. Both support the positive relationship between landing force and foraging success during hunting strikes, contrasting with sit-and-wait strategy. OpenEval emphasizes large sample sizes and confidence intervals; peer reviewer explicitly confirmed the finding.

Both support sex differences in body mass, provisioning, and hunting strategy (C36-C40). OpenEval notes internal consistency and descriptive statistics. Peer review R7 accepts these along with additional sex-based claims (C41-C49) that OpenEval evaluates separately.

OpenEval R9 supports sex differences in hunting success (C42-C44) with statistical documentation. Peer review R7 includes these claims in comprehensive acceptance of sex-based differences without separate discussion.
OpenEval R10 supports differential patterns in landing force by sex (C45-C48) and reversal when normalized. Peer review R7 includes these in overall acceptance of sex differences.
OpenEval R11 supports C49 (small but significant sex difference in landing force). Peer review R7 includes this claim in comprehensive acceptance of sex-based findings.
OpenEval R12 supports C41 (sex difference in hunting attempt rate) as supporting observation. Peer review R7 includes this in overall acceptance of sex differences.

Both support comparative findings (C56, C74-C75) but OpenEval explicitly notes sampling rate limitation (C78) suggesting conservative estimates. Peer review R6 accepts comparison without challenging limitations. Peer review also includes C76-C79 which OpenEval addresses separately.

OpenEval R17 explicitly supports C78 as correctly identifying methodological limitation (50 Hz sampling rate). Peer review R6 includes C78 among accepted claims without separate discussion of this limitation.
OpenEval R18 supports dual function interpretation (C77, C79) as reasonable inference. Peer review R6 includes these claims in overall acceptance of comparative findings.

Key divergence: OpenEval supports primary conclusions (C53, C57-C60, C124) but notes acoustic camouflage interpretation is inferential since study measures force not sound. Peer reviewers fully endorsed the acoustic camouflage interpretation without this caveat, with editor stating work 'provides new corroboration for motion-induced sound camouflage.'

Significant divergence: OpenEval rates C62-C67 as UNCERTAIN, noting they are 'largely speculative interpretations' lacking direct evidence. Peer review R9 accepts these interpretations as supported, stating 'results support the authors' conclusion.' This represents the most substantial disagreement between evaluations.

Significant divergence: OpenEval rates mechanistic explanations (C70, C72-C73, C80-C86) as UNCERTAIN, calling them 'speculative' and noting they 'go beyond what the data directly demonstrate.' Peer reviewers accepted these interpretations without challenge, finding evidence 'compelling.'

OpenEval supports ecological implications (C87-C90) with C87 well-supported and C89-C90 as reasonable extrapolations requiring further testing. Peer review R9 accepts these broader implications, noting 'broad implications for understanding predator-prey interactions' without distinguishing which require additional testing.

OpenEval R20 evaluates literature-based context claims (C1-C16, C68-C69, C71, C76) as appropriately cited and supporting the study's rationale. No corresponding separate peer review evaluation found; these background claims were implicitly accepted.
